reason: The sources provide sufficient dual-sourced factual details about the discovery, scale, structure, and competing glowing mechanisms of Lyman-alpha blobs.
story: Deep in the early universe, billions of light-years away, float some of the largest single objects in the cosmos: Lyman-alpha blobs. Discovered in 2000 by astronomer Chuck Steidel and his team, these colossal clouds of glowing hydrogen gas span up to 400,000 light-years across—more than four times the width of our Milky Way galaxy. Using the Subaru Telescope, astronomer Yuichi Matsuda found over 30 more of these giant blobs aligned along a mind-boggling cosmic web stretching over 200 million light-years. But what makes these behemoths shine? While scientists debated whether gravity was pulling in cooling gas or supernova winds were blowing out material, observations from the Very Large Telescope solved part of the puzzle for LAB-1. By measuring polarized light, astronomers discovered that hidden galaxies and supermassive black holes inside the blobs act as cosmic light bulbs, illuminating the vast clouds from within.
angle: Lyman-alpha blobs are gigantic clouds of hydrogen gas spanning up to 400,000 light-years across—four times the size of the Milky Way—and lining cosmic structures over 200 million light-years long.

claims.claim: Lyman-alpha blobs are immense concentrations of glowing hydrogen gas in deep space.
Lyman-alpha blobs rank among the largest known individual objects in the Universe.
Some individual Lyman-alpha blobs span 300,000 to 400,000 light-years across.
Lyman-alpha blobs are several times larger than the Milky Way galaxy, which measures under 100,000 light-years across.
The prominent Lyman-alpha blob known as LAB-1 was discovered in the year 2000.
Astronomer Steidel and colleagues published early discovery findings on Lyman-alpha blobs in 2000.
Astronomer Yuichi Matsuda and a team using the Subaru Telescope discovered more than 30 additional Lyman-alpha blobs.
The discovered Lyman-alpha blobs trace out a colossal cosmic filament structure stretching over 200 million light-years.
Lyman-alpha blobs are located in the distant, high-redshift Universe, observed as they existed billions of years ago.
Astronomers developed multiple competing theories for what makes Lyman-alpha blobs glow, including infalling cool gas and central power sources.
Intense star formation and resulting supernova explosions blowing out gas were proposed as a potential mechanism for blob emission.
Active galaxies containing supermassive black holes were proposed as potential internal power sources driving blob emission.
Lyman-alpha radiation is a characteristic emission line produced by hydrogen gas.

disputed: The exact power mechanism producing Lyman-alpha emission across all blobs was historically disputed among gravitational heating, galactic superwinds, and central photoionization; script should present this as an ongoing scientific inquiry while noting that ESO VLT polarization measurements proved LAB-1 is powered by central embedded galaxies scattering light.
